beschreibung: Indian Ocean, Kolonialismus, British Empire und Legacy, Indentured Labour, Postkolonialismus und Sprachtraining.

p: The monsoon winds made the Indian Ocean a huge trade network long before Europeans arrived.

p: Merchants from East Africa, Arabia, Persia, India and Southeast Asia traded across the ocean.
Goods: spices, cotton and silk textiles, gold, ivory, pearls, porcelain.
Ships such as dhows used the seasonal winds.
cards.tag: Ergänzt, steht nicht in deinem Material

p: Europe: many small kingdoms, land and farming were central, the Church was powerful.
Indian Ocean: busy trade network with rich port cities and merchant cultures.
Islam and trade languages spread along the trade routes.
So the Indian Ocean region was often wealthier and more connected than Europe.
cards.tag: Ergänzt, steht nicht in deinem Material

p: Reasons: the monsoon, high demand for goods like spices and textiles, good ports, shared trade languages.
Effects: wealthy port cities, cultural and religious mixing, new languages like Swahili.
Later effect: Europeans wanted to control this profitable trade.
cards.tag: Ergänzt, steht nicht in deinem Material

p: Trade also spread religions, languages and food between coasts.
Many port cities are still mixed cultures today.
Europeans later entered this system, for example with trading companies like the East India Company (Buch S. 116).
Indentured labour replaced slave labour on many plantations, but conditions were often very hard.
cards.tag: Ergänzt, steht nicht in deinem Material

p: In 1807 Britain banned the slave trade, so it was no longer allowed to buy and ship enslaved people (Buch S. 116).
Plantations (sugar, cotton, tobacco, cocoa) still needed cheap workers.
So workers on contracts took the place of slaves.
cards.tag: Daten aus dem Buch, Verbindung ergänzt

p: A worker signed a contract (indenture) for several years, often five.
The employer paid the journey, the worker paid it back with work.
Many were recruited in India and shipped to places like Mauritius, Fiji, South Africa, the Caribbean and Guyana.
cards.tag: Ergänzt, steht nicht in deinem Material

p: Mauritius had sugar plantations that needed many workers.
Indian indentured labourers arrived there, for example at Aapravasi Ghat.
Many other places also received such workers, you don't need to know which.
cards.tag: Ergänzt, steht nicht in deinem Material

p: Descendants stayed and built communities abroad (the Indian diaspora).
Languages, food, festivals and religion spread to new places.
The system ended in the early 20th century.
cards.tag: Ergänzt, steht nicht in deinem Material

p: Reasons: slavery was abolished, plantations still needed cheap, controllable workers, poverty in India pushed people to sign.
Consequences for workers: low pay, hard work, little freedom, often a 'new form of slavery'.
Consequences for societies: new communities, mixed cultures, diaspora.

p: Whose story is told, and whose is missing?
Is the past celebrated, ignored or criticised?
Link: the question is not what British rule did for India, but what it did to them (Boodia-Canoo).
Colonialism means one country takes control of other lands and peoples, mainly for trade and profit.
cards.tag: Ergänzt, steht nicht in deinem Material

p: Modern European colonial history began with the discovery of the Americas in 1492.
Portuguese, Spanish, British, French, Dutch and Germans raced for claims.
After beating the Spanish Armada in 1588, British sea power grew.
Companies like the East India Company and the Hudson's Bay Company made huge profits.
From 1607 thirteen colonies were founded in North America, later the USA.
Britain: India, Australia, parts of Africa.
France: Algeria, West Africa. Belgium: Congo.
Portugal: Brazil, Angola, Mozambique. Spain: large parts of Latin America.
Germany: colonies in Africa, for example Namibia and Tanzania.

p: Economic: raw materials, new markets, huge trading profits (Buch S. 116).
Political: power and prestige, competition between European states.
Ideas: belief in Western superiority and a 'civilising mission' (Buch S. 116).
Strategic: bases and trade routes.
Exploitation of people and resources, slavery and forced labour.
Colonial languages and systems replaced or shaped local ones.
Borders drawn by Europeans, local cultures were pushed back.
Economic dependence on the colonial power.
Slaves captured in West Africa were shipped to the Caribbean and American colonies.
They worked on sugar, cotton, tobacco and cocoa plantations.
In 1807 Britain banned the slave trade. But people who were already enslaved stayed enslaved: slavery itself continued in the British Empire until 1834 and in the US until 1865.
1770 Captain Cook 'discovers' Australia, 1776 American Declaration of Independence.
1857 Indian Mutiny, 1876 Queen Victoria becomes Empress of India.
In 1920 the Empire covered a quarter of the Earth's land mass.
English became the official language, systems were shaped after the British model.
Britain believed in the dominance of Western civilisation and in 'civilising' people.
The East India Company traded in India and gained power.
1857: the Indian Mutiny was crushed with British troops.
1876: Queen Victoria became Empress of India.
English, law, education and transport followed the British model.
1947: India became independent.
The British Empire was seen as unbeatable around 1906, but it changed into the Commonwealth, and its legacy is still debated.
Churchill: around 1906 Britain's power seemed secure and permanent, protected by the Royal Navy.
George VI: the Empire became a family of free nations, united by loyalty to the Crown.
Malcolm X: the huge Empire was challenged even by 13 small colonies tired of taxation without representation.
Olusoga: losing the American colonies started a nostalgic longing for lost wealth and influence.
Jamrozik: empire builders justified their actions with a belief in their own superiority.

cards.h: George V and the changing Empire
p: King and Emperor of India from 1910 to 1936.
His reign saw the rise of socialism, communism, fascism, Irish republicanism and the Indian independence movement.
After the First World War the Empire reached its greatest extent.
1917: the royal house was renamed Windsor because of anti-German feeling.
An organisation of 53 independent states, almost all former parts of the Empire.
The British monarch is its ceremonial head.
Secretariat founded in 1965, based in London (Marlborough House).
About 2.1 billion people, a third of the world, and about 20% of world trade.
Largest members: Canada, Australia, India.
Values: equality, peace, liberty, human rights, free trade (Singapore Declaration 1971, Harare Declaration 1991).
Some stress order, trade and the Commonwealth.
Others stress exploitation, slavery and racism.
Nostalgia for the Empire still plays a role in British debates.
Your own opinion with reasons is important.
Postcolonialism asks how colonial rule still shapes societies today.

p: In Bengaluru protesters tore down English billboards and demanded Kannada.
A law should make 60% of each sign Kannada.
India has more than 300 languages, states were formed along language lines.
Locals fear becoming a minority and losing jobs, many migrants come from outside.
Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (warriors), Vaishyas (traders), Shudras (labourers).
Dalits, once called 'untouchables', are outside the system and face severe discrimination.
Untouchability is abolished by the constitution, but atrocities still happen daily.
Over 130,000 anti-Dalit crimes were registered between 2018 and 2020.
The video links colonial famines to diabetes in south Asians.
Bodies adapted to starvation and store sugar as fat.
Risk of diabetes, obesity and heart disease is higher and passes to children and grandchildren.
The question is not what British rule did for India.
The question is what British rule did to them.
She compares colonised people to survivors of abuse: loss is real, but nobody can measure it exactly.
India became independent in 1947.
English stayed important: official language, education, law, politics, jobs.
Social problems like caste discrimination remain, even if officially banned.
Debate: who benefited from colonialism, and what did it do to people?
You give a presentation (monologue) on a topic, using a visual such as a photo, cartoon or chart.
Then you answer questions.
Don't read from a script. Use prompt cards with key words.
1 Greet: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen.
2 Introduce yourself: Let me introduce myself. My name is ...
3 Topic: The subject of my presentation is ...
4 Outline: My talk is divided into three parts. Firstly, ... Secondly, ... and thirdly, ...
5 Part 1: Let me start by telling you about ...
6 Part 2: Now I'll move on to the second part.
7 Part 3: This brings me to my final point.
8 Summarise: So, to summarise, ...
9 Thank: Thank you all for listening.
10 Questions: If you have any questions, I'd be happy to answer them now.
State the type (photo, cartoon, ...) and say what you can see in one sentence.
Give the setting (time and place) in the simple present.
Describe in detail: people, objects, foreground, background.
Use the present progressive for actions.
Analyse: look at people, symbols, texts (who speaks to whom?), the source and context.
State the message and the addressee, give reasons.
Evaluate: give your opinion with reasons, refer to your own experience.
Comment on effectiveness: importance, comprehensibility, humour, appeal.
Type, theme (title), numbers, units, categories, time frame, x- and y-axis, source.
Focus on maximum and minimum points and trends. You might compare two charts.
Consider the author's intention and the importance of the data.
Short conclusion: It can be seen from the chart that ...
I didn't quite understand why ...
Would you tell us a little bit more about ...
What exactly do you mean by ...
Could you explain how to ...
Do you happen to know how ...
I was wondering whether you could tell us ...
Don't know: I'm afraid I don't have the answer to that.
Repeat: You'll remember I said earlier that ...
Ask for repetition: Sorry, I didn't catch your question.
Ask back: That's an interesting question. Could I ask you what you think?
Other words: To put it another way, ...
Thinking time: I'm glad you asked me that question.
Add something: Can I throw in my two cents?
Disagree politely: I beg to differ.
Show understanding: I see what you're trying to say.
Challenge: I get your point, but have you tried to view it from the perspective of ...?
Ask for opinion: What's your opinion on this issue?
Agree with the other side when their arguments are good.
Oh, yeah, I haven't thought about it that way, nonetheless I believe it's more important to ...
Agree with your partner beforehand on how to structure the discussion.
End with a conclusion or a compromise.
On the same page: agreeing with each other.
A double-edged sword: something with pros and cons.
More ideas: It's a win-win situation. / On the one hand ..., on the other hand ... / At the end of the day, ...
Use idioms only if you are sure how they work.

p: Trade, power and memory connect the Indian Ocean, colonialism and postcolonial societies.
cards.tag: Ergänzt, steht nicht in deinem Material

p: Indian Ocean trade existed before Europeans, driven by the monsoon.
Europeans entered it with trading companies and colonies.
Slavery ended and indentured labour supplied cheap workers.
Colonial rule shaped language, systems and inequality, for example in India.
Memory and postcolonialism ask how we remember this past and what it did to people.
cards.tag: Ergänzt, steht nicht in deinem Material

p: Structure: greet, introduce, topic, outline, three parts, summary, thanks, questions.
With a visual: describe, analyse, evaluate.
Always give your opinion with reasons.

quiz.q: What drove sailing ships across the Indian Ocean?
quiz.a: The seasonal monsoon winds
quiz.e: Sailors used the monsoon, which changes direction with the seasons.

quiz.q: Which was a typical Indian Ocean trade good?
quiz.a: Spices
quiz.e: Spices, textiles, gold, ivory and pearls were traded.

quiz.q: Who took part in Indian Ocean trade before the Europeans came?
quiz.a: Merchants from Africa, Arabia, India and Southeast Asia
quiz.e: The network existed long before Europeans entered it.

quiz.q: Which British company is named in the book for trade with India?
quiz.a: The East India Company
quiz.e: The Royal African Company is named for the slave trade.

quiz.q: What is an indentured labourer?
quiz.a: A worker bound by a contract for a fixed time
falsch: A free worker who picks a new employer every day
A soldier of a trading company
quiz.e: The contract (indenture) tied the worker to the employer for several years.

quiz.q: Why were indentured labourers needed after slavery ended?
quiz.a: Plantations still needed cheap workers
falsch: Owners wanted to pay high wages
quiz.e: Sugar, cotton and tobacco plantations still made big profits.

quiz.q: When was the British slave trade abolished?
quiz.e: Slavery itself continued in the Empire until 1834 and in the US until 1865.

quiz.q: When did slavery itself end in the British Empire?
quiz.e: In 1807 the slave trade was banned. In 1834 slavery itself ended in the British Empire. In the US slavery ended in 1865.

quiz.q: Where were Indian indentured labourers sent?
quiz.a: To plantations, for example in Mauritius, Fiji or the Caribbean
quiz.e: They were shipped across the empire where cheap workers were needed.

quiz.q: What is a long-term result of indentured labour?
quiz.a: Large communities of Indian descent abroad
falsch: The end of trade in the Indian Ocean
quiz.e: This is often called the Indian diaspora.

quiz.q: What does 'memory' mean here?
quiz.a: How a society remembers and talks about its past
quiz.e: Memory includes museums, stories, food, music and debates.

quiz.q: Which question fits memory analysis best?
quiz.a: Whose story is told and whose is missing?
quiz.e: Memory is about perspective and about what is left out.

quiz.q: What is Aapravasi Ghat?
quiz.a: A site in Mauritius where indentured labourers arrived
quiz.e: It is a memorial site for indentured labour.

quiz.q: Modern European colonial history began with ...
quiz.a: the discovery of the Americas in 1492
quiz.e: Then Europeans raced for claims in the 'New World'.

quiz.q: What happened in 1588?
quiz.a: Britain defeated the Spanish Armada
falsch: Queen Victoria became Empress of India
quiz.e: After that British power at sea increased steadily.

quiz.q: What led to the Declaration of Independence in 1776?
quiz.a: A rebellion over a tea tax
falsch: The end of the slave trade
quiz.e: The thirteen colonies later became the USA.

quiz.q: Who 'discovered' Australia in 1770?
quiz.a: Captain James Cook
quiz.e: The first colonies in Australia were prison colonies.

quiz.q: What title did Queen Victoria receive in 1876?
quiz.a: Empress of India
quiz.e: The British parliament named her so.

quiz.q: How much of the Earth's land did the Empire cover in 1920?
quiz.a: A quarter
quiz.e: It ran from Canada to Australia and from Egypt to South Africa.

quiz.q: What was a lasting effect of British rule in its colonies?
quiz.a: English became the official language and systems followed the British model
falsch: All colonies kept their old systems
Every colony became a republic at once
Local languages were made official everywhere
quiz.e: Education, law, politics and transport were shaped by Britain.

quiz.q: What did slaves from West Africa do in the colonies?
quiz.a: Worked on sugar, cotton, tobacco and cocoa plantations
quiz.e: Their products were brought back to Britain.

quiz.q: Who are the Dalits?
quiz.a: People outside the caste system, once called 'untouchables'
quiz.e: Brahmins are priests, Kshatriyas warriors, Vaishyas traders, Shudras labourers.

quiz.q: Which caste group is at the top of the system?
quiz.a: Brahmins
quiz.e: They are traditionally priests and scholars.

quiz.q: Why did protesters tear down English billboards in Bengaluru?
quiz.a: They wanted signs in the local language, Kannada
quiz.e: A law should make 60% of each sign Kannada.

quiz.q: How many languages does India have according to the BBC article?
quiz.a: More than 300
quiz.e: States were formed along language lines after independence.

quiz.q: What fear lies behind the 'Kannada first' demand?
quiz.a: Locals fear becoming a minority and losing jobs
quiz.e: Four out of ten people in Bengaluru come from outside the city.

quiz.q: What is Boodia-Canoo's key question?
quiz.a: What did British rule do to them?
falsch: What did British rule do for India?
How many colonies did Britain have?
quiz.e: She says the benefits question is like asking how abuse survivors benefit from their abusers.

quiz.q: How does the video link colonialism and diabetes?
quiz.a: Famine adaptation raised the risk of diabetes in south Asians
quiz.e: Bodies adapted to starvation store sugar as fat, the risk passes to children.

quiz.q: How many anti-Dalit crimes were registered between 2018 and 2020?
quiz.e: The highest number was reported from Uttar Pradesh.

quiz.q: Which phrase opens a presentation?
quiz.a: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen.
falsch: This brings me to my final point.
quiz.e: Step 1 is to greet the audience.

quiz.q: Which phrase outlines the structure?
quiz.a: My talk is divided into three parts.
falsch: Sorry, I didn't catch your question.
quiz.e: Outline comes after the topic.

quiz.q: Which phrase starts the ending?
quiz.a: So, to summarise, ...
falsch: Let me start by telling you about ...
Now I'll move on to the second part.
quiz.e: Then thank the audience and invite questions.

quiz.q: What do you say if you don't know the answer?
quiz.a: I'm afraid I don't have the answer to that.
falsch: Sorry, I didn't catch your question.
I'm glad you asked me that question.
quiz.e: The other phrases ask for repetition, rephrase or buy time.

quiz.q: How do you ask someone to repeat a question?
quiz.a: Sorry, I didn't catch your question.
falsch: You'll remember I said earlier that ...
quiz.e: You can also ask: Did you say 'when' or 'where'?

quiz.q: What is the first point when describing a visual?
quiz.a: State the type of visual and say what you can see in one sentence
falsch: State the message and the addressee
Name the source in a footnote
quiz.e: Description comes first, then analysis, then evaluation.

quiz.q: Which tenses do you use to describe a visual?
quiz.a: Simple present for the setting, present progressive for actions
quiz.e: Example: The photo shows a street. People are walking.

quiz.q: How can you end a chart description?
quiz.a: It can be seen from the chart that ...
falsch: I hope you liked my picture.
quiz.e: Add a short conclusion after naming maximum, minimum and trends.

quiz.q: What is a good tip for the oral exam?
quiz.a: Use prompt cards with key words instead of reading a script
quiz.e: Speak slowly, clearly and naturally.

quiz.q: How did the Indian Ocean region compare to Europe between 500 and 1500?
quiz.a: It was a busy, connected trade network with rich port cities
falsch: It was an isolated region without trade
It was ruled by one European empire
It was poorer than Europe in every way
quiz.e: Europe was split into many kingdoms, the Indian Ocean was highly connected.

quiz.q: Which is a reason for the rise of the Indian Ocean trade system?
quiz.a: The monsoon and high demand for goods like spices
quiz.e: Regular winds and demand for goods made long trade routes possible.

quiz.q: Which is an effect of Indian Ocean trade on the region?
quiz.a: Wealthy port cities and cultural and religious mixing
falsch: The end of all languages but one
A single ruler for the whole ocean
quiz.e: Islam and languages like Swahili spread along the coasts.

quiz.q: Which country colonised the Congo?
quiz.a: Belgium
quiz.e: France took Algeria, Portugal Brazil and Angola, Spain much of Latin America.

quiz.q: Which is an economic reason for colonisation?
quiz.a: Raw materials and new markets
quiz.e: Trading profits attracted the European powers.

quiz.q: What was the 'civilising mission'?
quiz.a: The belief that Western civilisation should be brought to 'wild peoples'
falsch: A plan to build schools without any control
quiz.e: It was used to justify colonial rule.

quiz.q: Which is an effect of colonisation?
quiz.a: Exploitation, colonial languages and economic dependence
falsch: Full independence for all colonies at once
quiz.e: Colonised societies were shaped by the colonial power.

quiz.q: When did India become independent?
quiz.e: 1857 was the Mutiny, 1876 Victoria became Empress.

quiz.q: Which island is the main example for indentured labour in your class?
quiz.a: Mauritius
quiz.e: Indian workers arrived there for the sugar plantations.

quiz.q: Why did people in India sign indenture contracts?
quiz.a: Poverty pushed them to look for work and a better life
falsch: They wanted to rule the plantations
They were forced by no one at all
They wanted to join the army
quiz.e: But many did not know how hard conditions would be.

quiz.q: How does the English language still shape India?
quiz.a: It remains important in education, law and jobs
falsch: It is only used on stamps
quiz.e: The Bengaluru debate shows the tension over English and local languages.

quiz.q: How many member states does the Commonwealth have according to your book?
quiz.e: All but three were formerly part of the British Empire.

quiz.q: Who is the ceremonial head of the Commonwealth?
quiz.a: The British monarch
quiz.e: The position is ceremonial and representative.

quiz.q: Where is the Commonwealth Secretariat based?
quiz.a: London, at Marlborough House
quiz.e: It was established in 1965.

quiz.q: Which are the three largest Commonwealth members?
quiz.a: Canada, Australia and India
quiz.e: The Commonwealth covers all six inhabited continents.

quiz.q: About what share of the world's population lives in the Commonwealth?
quiz.a: About one third
quiz.e: That is roughly 2.1 billion people.

quiz.q: When were the Commonwealth Games first held?
quiz.a: 1939 (since then every four years)
quiz.e: Sports include netball and rugby.

quiz.q: What happened to the British Empire after the First World War?
quiz.a: It expanded to its greatest extent
quiz.e: The empires of Russia and Germany fell, the British Empire grew.

quiz.q: Which royal house name was chosen in 1917?
quiz.a: Windsor
quiz.e: It replaced Saxe-Coburg and Gotha because of anti-German feeling in WWI.

quiz.q: What does Jamrozik say about empire builders?
quiz.a: They justified their actions by believing in their own superiority
falsch: They acted only out of charity
quiz.e: He says that in the British Empire God was an Englishman.

quiz.q: What started the 'nostalgic yearning' for the Empire, according to Olusoga?
quiz.a: The loss of the American colonies
falsch: The end of the Cold War
quiz.e: It became part of the national psyche.

quiz.q: Which phrase do you use to add something to the discussion?
quiz.a: Can I throw in my two cents?
quiz.e: It means adding your opinion to the conversation.

quiz.q: Which phrase politely shows you disagree?
quiz.a: I beg to differ.
falsch: I get your point, we are on the same page.
Can I throw in my two cents?
quiz.e: It sounds polite and formal.

quiz.q: What does 'a double-edged sword' mean?
quiz.a: Something with pros and cons
quiz.e: Example: Social media is a double-edged sword.

quiz.q: What does 'we are on the same page' mean?
quiz.a: We agree
quiz.e: Useful when you want to show agreement.

quiz.q: What makes a discussion sound like a real conversation?
quiz.a: Agreeing with good points of your partner
quiz.e: Then a conclusion or compromise at the end sounds natural.

karten.begriff: I see what you're trying to say.
karten.erklaerung: Shows understanding before you give your own view.

karten.begriff: I get your point, but have you tried to view it from the perspective of ...?
karten.erklaerung: Challenge the other view politely.

karten.begriff: What's your opinion on this issue?
karten.erklaerung: Asks your partner for their view.
Idiom: agreeing with each other.
Idiom: something with pros and cons.

klausur.q: Describe the map 'The British Empire in 1920' (Buch S. 116) as you would at the start of an oral exam.
punkte: Type: a map, theme: the British Empire in 1920
Green areas show the Empire, the rest is grey
Large areas: Canada, India, Australia, parts of Africa and the Middle East
Source: textbook, 'A brief history of (post)colonial times'
Message: the Empire had a huge reach, a quarter of the Earth's land mass

klausur.q: Explain what indentured labour was and why it was introduced.
punkte: Workers signed a contract for a fixed time, often five years
Slavery had ended (the slave trade was banned in 1807, slavery itself in 1834)
Plantations still needed cheap workers
Workers were recruited in India and shipped overseas
Conditions were often hard

klausur.q: Explain why the Indian Ocean was important for trade.
punkte: Monsoon winds allowed regular sailing
Many regions were connected: Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia
Spices, textiles, gold, ivory were traded
Religions, languages and food spread
Europeans later wanted to control the routes
Similarity: cheap labour on plantations, hard conditions
Difference: indentured labourers signed contracts for a fixed time
Slaves were owned and had no end date
Both are linked to colonial profit
Conclusion with your own judgement

klausur.q: Explain what 'Indian Ocean memory' means and give an example.
punkte: Memory means how a society remembers its past
Topics: trade, slavery, indentured labour
Example: Aapravasi Ghat memorial in Mauritius, or food, music, Creole languages
Whose story is told, whose is missing

klausur.q: Analyse how the colonial past still shapes India today. Use the language debate in Bengaluru or the caste system.
punkte: English as colonial language still plays a role (jobs, IT, Bengaluru)
Kannada protesters want local language on signs (60% law)
Over 300 languages, tension between regions and migrants
Caste: untouchability is abolished, but atrocities against Dalits continue
Link to colonial legacy and your own conclusion

klausur.q: 'The question is what British rule did to them.' Evaluate this statement by Boodia-Canoo.
punkte: She rejects asking what British rule did for India
Comparison: survivors of abuse and their abusers
Harm and loss cannot be measured exactly, but are real
Argument against: some effects like English or railways had benefits
Own opinion with reasons

klausur.q: Discuss whether former colonial powers should deal more with their colonial past, for example in schools and museums.
punkte: Pro: truth, respect for victims, understanding of today's inequality
Pro: memory shapes identity
Contra: guilt of people today, focus on the future
Contra: complicated history, risk of one-sided views
Conclusion with your own opinion

klausur.q: Give a short talk (about two minutes) on colonialism, using the ten-step structure.
punkte: Greeting and introduction
Topic and outline in three parts
Part 1: early colonies and trade
Part 2: slave trade, plantations and indentured labour
Part 3: legacy today
Summary, thanks, invite questions

klausur.q: Explain how English became so important in the former colonies.
punkte: Britain believed in the dominance of Western civilisation
English was made the official language
Education, law, politics, economy and transport followed the British model
Today English still matters for jobs and business

klausur.q: You get a cartoon about colonialism. Evaluate how effective it is.
punkte: State type, setting and what you see
Analyse symbols, text, source and message
Name the addressee
Comment on importance, comprehensibility, humour, appeal
Give your own opinion with reasons

klausur.q: Compare the situation in Europe and the Indian Ocean region between 500 and 1500.
punkte: Europe: small kingdoms, farming, powerful Church
Indian Ocean: busy trade, rich port cities
Trade spread religion and languages in the Indian Ocean
The Indian Ocean was often wealthier and more connected
Own conclusion

klausur.q: Explain reasons for and effects of the colonisation of non-European countries by Europeans.
punkte: Reasons: profit, raw materials, markets
Reasons: power, prestige, competition, belief in 'civilising'
Effects: exploitation, slavery, forced labour
Effects: colonial language and systems, borders, dependence
Example: India and England

klausur.q: Explain the system of indentured labour with its reasons and consequences. Use Mauritius as an example.
punkte: Reason: slavery abolished, plantations need cheap workers
Workers recruited with contracts, shipped overseas
Mauritius: sugar plantations, workers from India
Consequences: hard conditions, little freedom
Consequences: new communities, mixed cultures, diaspora

klausur.q: Describe the Commonwealth of Nations (Buch, Info-Kasten).
punkte: 53 independent member states, almost all former parts of the Empire
British monarch is ceremonial head
Secretariat founded 1965, based in London
2.1 billion people, a third of the world, about 20% of world trade
Largest members: Canada, Australia, India
Values: equality, peace, liberty, human rights, free trade

klausur.q: Analyse the different views of the British Empire in the quotations by Churchill, George VI, Malcolm X, Olusoga and Jamrozik.
punkte: Churchill: Empire secure and permanent, pride
George VI: free nations united by loyalty to the Crown
Malcolm X: critical view, oppression and resistance
Olusoga: nostalgia after losing colonies
Jamrozik: belief in superiority as a justification
Link the views to the speakers' backgrounds

klausur.q: Discuss whether Britain should be proud of its Empire.
punkte: Pro: trade, Commonwealth, spread of English and institutions
Contra: slavery, exploitation, racism, violence (for example 1857)
Perspective of the colonised, for example Boodia-Canoo
Nostalgia versus critical memory
Conclusion with your own opinion

klausur.q: With a partner, discuss: 'Colonialism had only negative effects.' Aim for a conclusion at the end.
punkte: Structure agreed with your partner
Own opinion with reasons and examples
Agree with good arguments of your partner
Polite disagreement (I beg to differ ...)
Use of at least one idiom
Final conclusion or compromise

operatoren.name: Describe
operatoren.text: Present the facts in an organised way.

operatoren.name: Explain
operatoren.text: Make a topic clear with reasons and examples.

operatoren.name: Analyse
operatoren.text: Break a topic down and show how the parts connect.

operatoren.name: Evaluate
operatoren.text: Weigh arguments and give your own judgement with reasons.

operatoren.name: Discuss
operatoren.text: Weigh pro and contra and reach a conclusion.
